title: The Word as Guru
hookLine: the Guru is not a body but the Word

cards: A gathering of yogis, men who had left the world behind to master the body and the breath. A traveler walks into their circle, and they start testing him. Who are you?
Where do you come from? What path are you on? You met these yogis on their mountain back in year one.
Their conversation is in the Granth, a long hymn called Siddh Gosht, the talk with the Siddhas. Near its heart, they ask him straight out: who is your guru? Whose disciple are you?

teach.h: THE YOGIS ASK: WHO IS YOUR GURU?
teach.b: For a seeker in the yogis' circle, a guru would be a person: a teacher you sat before, served and followed.

teach.h: THE WORD IS GURU; ATTENTION, DISCIPLE.
teach.b: Guru Nanak's answer, in paraphrase: the shabad, the Word, is the guru, and the surat, attention tuned to its sound, is the disciple. Yesterday's word is right there in the answer.
The disciple isn't a body at a teacher's feet. It's attention, turned toward the Word. And the guru isn't a body either.
Guru Ram Das says it plainly.
In paraphrase: the bani is the Guru, and the Guru is the bani, and within the bani are all the nectars. Bani is the Word as it comes through the Gurus' hymns.
He doesn't say the bani is like the Guru, or speaks for the Guru. He says it is the Guru. Think what that means.
A teacher in a body can be far away, asleep, busy, or gone.

teach.h: A TEACHER ALWAYS IN THE ROOM.
teach.b: A teacher who is the Word can be opened at dawn, sung in a kitchen, remembered in a hospital waiting room. It doesn't age.
And it doesn't flatter: bring it a question, and it answers in its own words, not the ones you hoped for.
So when Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, they understand themselves to be bowing to the Word, not to paper and ink.

how: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, understanding the Guru to be the Word, the bani, rather than a human body, and take daily guidance by reading from it.

games.q: what does “the word as guru” mean?
o: a spoken blessing given at the end of a service
the Guru as the Word itself, not a person's body
a rule that only priests may read the scripture

games.q: the Word as Guru: tap the pairs.
p: the guru, in Guru Nanak's answer
the disciple, in Guru Nanak's answer

s: in the Siddh Gosht, Guru Nanak names a human teacher as his guru
he answers that the Word is the guru and attention is the disciple.
Guru Ram Das says within the bani are all the nectars
the bani is the Guru, and the Guru is the bani.
Sikhs bow to the Granth as paper and ink
they understand themselves to be bowing to the Word.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, and a circle of yogis asks: who is your guru? whose disciple are you? what do you answer?
o: name the teacher I studied with as a boy.
the Word is my guru; my attention is its disciple.
I have no guru and need none.
games.why: in the Siddh Gosht, Guru Nanak answers that the shabad is the guru and the surat, attention tuned to it, is the disciple.

practice: Hold one line from the Granth you already know, and if none comes, take the opening, Ik Onkar, One Creator.

Sit with it the way you'd sit before a teacher, ask it one honest question about your day, and keep your surat on the line without making up an answer. Some days a line says something; some days it just keeps you company.

wordCard.voice: The Word as Guru. In the Siddh Gosht, the shabad is the guru and attention is the disciple; Guru Ram Das says the bani is the Guru. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the word teaches. A teacher who is always in the room. Until tomorrow.
